name: Texas Muslim Womens Foundation Inc
mission: Founded in 2005, Texas Muslim Women's Foundation (TMWF) aims to empower, promote and support all women and their families, with a special focus on North Texas. We are an equal opportunity provider. We engage all members of the community – women, men, seniors, families and youth through our various programs. We provide social and family violence services that foster peace and well-being in the home through our Peace in the Home Services and Peaceful Oasis Shelter. In addition, TMWF also arranges leadership skills development for Muslim youth to inspire the next generation to build a promising future for our society and educational programs for Muslim and non-Muslim community members to learn about topics essential to individual and community welfare.
theoryOfChange: By providing a holistic approach—combining immediate crisis shelter with long-term transitional housing, legal aid, and economic empowerment—survivors can move from crisis to independence.

rich_narrative.summary: The Texas Muslim Womens Foundation (TMWF) is a specialized social service provider dedicated to improving the well-being of families in North Texas. <cite id="1">founded in 2005</cite>, the organization has spent nearly two decades addressing critical community needs through a faith-sensitive lens. In FY2024, the foundation reported <cite id="2">total revenue of $3,769,366</cite>, representing a <cite id="3">19% decline from the previous year's revenue</cite> of $4,665,216. Despite this recent financial contraction, the organization maintains a <cite id="4">high program expense ratio of 86.0%</cite> according to Charity Navigator, ensuring that the vast majority of donor funds directly support community programs. TMWF operates with exceptional leaness, spending only <cite id="5">$0.03 to raise every $1</cite> in donations. Their work is primarily focused on domestic violence intervention, youth leadership, and senior support. In FY2024 alone, the foundation provided <cite id="6">emergency shelter to 137 residents</cite> and assisted <cite id="7">216 non-residential domestic violence clients</cite>. The organization is <cite id="8">zakat-eligible</cite>, serving specific categories including the poor (fuqara) and needy (masakin). While the foundation demonstrates strong programmatic efficiency, it faces governance challenges, most notably a <cite id="9">board size of only two members</cite>, which is significantly below standard nonprofit best practices for oversight.
